mcqs.question: A release is about to ship, and you must prove in a production-like environment that error tracking works end to end. Which check actually exercises the full path?
options: Throw `new Error('verify')` from the DevTools console of the deployed site and watch for the issue in the project.
Confirm at startup that `Sentry.init` ran without warnings and that the deployed bundle contains the SDK code.
Send a test event to the same DSN from a Node script running on a laptop, and check that the project receives it.
Trigger a clearly labeled error from an application handler in that environment, then check the issue's `environment` and `release`.
mcqs.explanation: Only an error raised by application code travels the whole path: the SDK's global handlers, the breadcrumb buffer, the transport, and the environment and release tags attached at init — and the arrived event is what you then inspect for symbolicated frames. The strongest distractor is the console throw: code typed into DevTools is evaluated in the console's own context and never reaches the `window` handlers the SDK hooks, so a missing issue proves nothing and an arriving issue tested none of your handlers. Startup warnings and a bundled SDK only show the library loaded; a Node script tests a different runtime, with no release tag from this build and no browser path to the user.

mcqs.question: Checkout emits ten `console.log` lines per order, including the whole `user` object and the full cart. During an incident nobody can filter by order, count how many checkouts took over two seconds, or tell a recovered failure from a success. Which redesign fixes the logging?
options: Log at `debug` at the top of every function and keep debug output enabled in production, so that no piece of state is ever missing from the transcript.
Emit one event per finished checkout with stable fields (`order_id`, `item_count`, `duration_ms`, `outcome`), severity set by actionability, and PII redacted before transport.
Emit one `error`-level line per failure and nothing on success, because a checkout that worked carries no diagnostic value during an incident.
Emit a single JSON string per attempt that embeds the full request and response payloads, so the exact state of any order can be read back later.
mcqs.explanation: Structured guidance is one wide event per operation with stable keys: `outcome` and `duration_ms` make checkouts countable and aggregatable, `order_id` takes an engineer from a support ticket to the event, and severity encodes what a human must act on. The strongest distractor is debug-everywhere: volume destroys the signal, the lines still have no stable fields to filter or aggregate, and debug output enabled in production is the specific anti-pattern — you get more text, not more answers. Errors-only loses the population (no failure rate, no slow successes, and when everything is `error` nothing stands out), and a single JSON blob with whole payloads adds personal data and cardinality while staying unqueryable as text.

mcqs.question: According to Google's recommended passing view, a page passes Core Web Vitals when which measurement meets the good thresholds?
options: The average of all field loads: LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, CLS at or under 0.1.
A Lighthouse lab score of 90 or higher on the reference device in CI.
The median field value per metric, allowing 10 percent of visits to fail without consequence.
The 75th percentile of field (RUM) data: LCP at or under 2.5 seconds, INP at or under 200 milliseconds, CLS at or under 0.1.
mcqs.explanation: The passing view is explicitly the 75th percentile of field data meeting each metric's threshold, because Core Web Vitals measure the proportion of visits with a good experience. The strongest distractor is the average: averages hide the tail, so a healthy average can coexist with many users having an unacceptable experience. Lab scores answer a different, controlled question, and neither averages nor medians express the share of users below the threshold.

mcqs.question: CI Lighthouse reports a clean run on the product page: CLS 0.00 and TBT 90 ms. Field data for the same page and release shows CLS 0.14 and INP 380 ms at p75. What explains the gap?
options: The field numbers are wrong: Lighthouse fixes the device and viewport, so its CLS is the authoritative measurement for that page and should override the beacon.
Both can be true: the lab run is one controlled load with no real interaction (so INP is unmeasurable there and TBT stands in), and it ends before late content shifts the layout.
TBT is the field version of INP, so the 380 ms is TBT measured on real devices and both tools are timing the same user experience under different names.
The two should agree, so a gap that large means either the RUM beacon is sampling failures or the release never reached every user.
mcqs.explanation: Lab and field answer different questions and are expected to disagree: the lab run is one controlled load on one simulated device, it has no real interaction (INP cannot be measured there, TBT is the proxy), and it finishes at load — so a banner, late image or injected widget that shifts the layout afterwards is invisible to it, while field CLS includes it. The strongest distractor is 'Lighthouse is authoritative because it is controlled': control is precisely what removes real devices, networks and post-load shifts from the measurement, which is why its CLS can read 0.00 on a page users see jump. TBT is a lab-only proxy, not a field twin of INP, and expecting agreement mistakes a synthetic run for a user population.

mcqs.question: Events from release `a1b2c3d` still show minified frames while the current release symbolicates. The event carries `debug_id: 9f2c…`; the file the CDN serves for that release reports `debug_id: 4d81…`. What does that tell you?
options: Different bytes: the event came from an artifact the uploaded map does not cover, so check what is actually served and re-upload for that build.
Debug IDs expire when a newer release ships, so re-upload the old release's maps under the current release name to make those events symbolicate.
The maps must be published at a public URL next to the JS so the service can fetch them for releases that are no longer current.
Browsers cached the minified file from before the deploy, and flushing the CDN cache will let the service symbolicate those older events retroactively.
mcqs.explanation: Symbolication is per artifact: an event can only be mapped by the source map whose Debug ID matches the one baked into the bytes that produced it, so two different IDs under one release name mean the served file and the uploaded map are different builds — normally a post-build step, a different base directory or a CDN re-minification changing the bytes after the upload. The strongest distractor is public hosting: publishing maps exposes your original source to anyone who asks, it is the fix the guidance rules out, and it cannot explain a mismatch that is release-specific. A Debug ID is a UUID baked into the artifact, not a lease that expires when a newer release ships, and flushing a cache does not attach a map to events that already arrived.

mcqs.question: An alert pages on-call during every deploy because the error rate spikes briefly during rollout, then recovers. The team has started ignoring it. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the threshold from 1% to 5% so the rollout spike stops crossing it and the page only fires for bigger failures.
Silence the rule automatically during deploy windows, so a rollout never pages on-call and real incidents are read from dashboards.
Scope it to a decision: filter by environment and release, separate a new regression from the known baseline, and route the routine rollout signal to a ticket.
Delete the alert; an error-rate rule cannot tell a deploy from an incident, so the page is not worth maintaining.
mcqs.explanation: An alert is a decision with a person, a speed and an action: page only on what a human must change within minutes, and scope the rule so the expected rollout spike is distinguished from a new regression — environment and release filters do that, and the routine signal still needs a home (a ticket or channel) so it is not simply lost. The strongest distractor is silencing the rule during deploys: it removes the page exactly when the risk is highest, which is how a regression introduced by that very deploy ships unnoticed, turning one noisy alert into a blind spot. Raising the threshold hides noise and real regressions at the same time and slows detection; deleting the rule throws away a legitimate symptom of user pain.

mcqs.question: `POST /checkout` fails for roughly 1 in 2000 sessions with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'currency')`. It started with release `4f2a9c`, there is no local reproduction, and users keep failing. What is the correct first move?
options: Replay the affected users' recorded sessions and stored request payloads against staging until one of them reproduces the crash.
Wait until the failure count is large enough to be statistically solid before touching a release that works for 99.95% of sessions.
Preserve the affected cohort's evidence (release, route, browser, traces), mitigate behind a flag or rollback, then diff affected against unaffected sessions.
Ship a debug build that wraps the checkout path in a broad `try/catch` and logs the whole cart, so the next failure lands with full detail.
mcqs.explanation: Intermittent failures are conditional, so the work is finding the condition in the population: characterize the affected cohort, preserve what the current release already emitted, mitigate the user harm (flag or rollback), then diff affected against unaffected sessions to isolate the variable. The strongest distractor is shipping a debug build: a new build is a new release, so the telemetry already correlated to `4f2a9c` stops describing what users are running, and the throw may not reproduce at all on the changed code. Replaying recorded sessions against staging cannot recreate the server-side data shape behind `undefined.currency`, and waiting is not free when real users keep failing: one failure in 2000 sessions with a clean release correlation is already a pattern, not noise.

mcqs.question: Every service on the request path emits spans, but the backend shows a short trace per service with no shared timeline, and the browser's span is not the parent of the server's. What is missing?
options: More spans per service, so the backend has enough data points to stitch the per-service traces back together by timestamp.
Context propagation: the outgoing request must carry the trace context, so the next service joins the same trace with the incoming span as parent.
A higher sample rate, because dropped spans are what split one trace into several disconnected per-service traces.
Stable operation names, because the backend joins spans into one trace when their operation names and attributes match.
mcqs.explanation: A trace is assembled from context that travels with the request: the outgoing call must carry the trace ID, the current span as parent, and the sampling flags (W3C `traceparent`), so the next service continues the same trace instead of starting its own. The strongest distractor is the sample rate: sampling decides which traces survive, not whether the surviving spans connect, and the symptom here is disconnection, not missing data. More spans adds points that still share no trace ID — timestamp stitching is not how the tree is built, and it would misparent concurrent work. Stable operation names make traces comparable and searchable; they are not the join key.

mcqs.question: You are introducing session replay in a checkout flow that shows account details and card forms. Which rollout matches responsible-use guidance?
options: Record with `replaysSessionSampleRate: 1.0` and `replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0`, so every session is available when someone needs to debug it.
Record without masking and restrict the replay dashboard to the on-call team, since access control is what protects the recorded data.
Enable replay only in staging and treat production incidents as unreproducible, because recording real users is never acceptable.
Mask text, inputs and media, validate the rules on real flows, keep a low session rate with a high error rate, and link replays to errors, traces and release.
mcqs.explanation: Replay reconstructs the DOM, so it shows whatever the user typed: the order of decisions is policy, masking, sampling, correlation — mask text, inputs and media by default, validate the rules against your real account and checkout components (the leak is always the custom widget, never the demo page), keep a low session rate for exploration with a high error rate so failures are captured, and link each recording to its error, trace and release. The strongest distractor is the 100%/100% pair: it maximises cost, main-thread work and exposure for sessions nobody will ever watch, and it does not answer the privacy question at all — sampling is not masking. Access control alone still records and stores sensitive DOM, and staging-only replay removes the production value entirely, because the failures worth watching are the ones staging does not reproduce.

mcqs.question: During an incident, two teams' telemetry cannot be joined: one tags deploys as `version`, the other as `release`, the logs carry no trace ID, and severity means different things in each service. Which split belongs in an organization-wide observability contract?
options: Standardize the vendor, the SDK and the dashboards so every service looks identical, and leave field names, severity and alert routing to each team, whose domains differ.
Standardize vocabulary, minimum fields and ownership: trace context, release identity, severity semantics, artifact upload, sampling and retention defaults, plus alert ownership.
Standardize log wording and dashboards, and leave sampling, retention and alert ownership to each team, since both depend on that team's traffic and its budget.
Standardize only the retention window and the sampling rate per data class, leaving field names, severity and correlation to each team's framework.
mcqs.explanation: A contract standardizes meaning and join keys — canonical fields, trace context, release identity, severity semantics, artifact upload, sampling and retention defaults, and who owns which alert — and leaves the SDK, the backend and the dashboards replaceable, so a vendor swap does not rewrite the org's vocabulary or the way two teams' data joins. The strongest distractor is mandating one vendor and identical instrumentation: it produces uniformity of implementation with undefined semantics, which is exactly the state that made the incident unjoinable, and it couples the meaning of the telemetry to one backend. Standardizing wording and dashboards fixes presentation while sampling, retention and alert ownership — the things that decide what exists and who acts — stay unowned, and retention alone leaves the join keys and severity semantics to chance.

mcqs.question: Failed orders rose after a deploy, and nobody can tell whether the time is spent in the payment call or in the inventory call. Which use of the three signals is correct?
options: Add a counter and a timer around every function in every service and alert on all of them, so the exact function is always visible without needing a trace.
Use a metric to confirm and quantify the regression, open traces of affected requests to find the slow or failing span, and read the correlated logs of those same requests for the event detail.
Search the log stream for the word `error` across all services and rank services by number of matching lines; the service with the most lines is the cause.
Turn on session replay at 100% and watch recordings until the failure appears on screen.
mcqs.explanation: Each signal answers a different question: metrics detect and quantify a population-wide change, traces follow one request across boundaries and show which span spent the time, and logs explain the discrete event inside that request once you can select it. Only that combination both finds the regression (metric) and says where it happened (trace) with the detail to act on (logs). The strongest distractor is the log-volume triage: it sounds like "drill into logs", but ranking services by matching lines measures logging verbosity, not failure — a chatty healthy service outranks a silent broken one, and a slow request produces no `error` line at all. Per-function metrics everywhere explode cardinality and still do not reconstruct one request's path, and replay shows the browser side only, not where a backend call spent its time.

mcqs.question: After an optimization release, mean latency for `POST /checkout` drops 15% while p95 rises from 900 ms to 1.6 s, and slow-checkout reports increase. What is the most likely explanation, and what should you do?
options: The p95 is being dragged up by a handful of outliers; switch the dashboard to the median, which is robust, and treat the change as noise until it persists for a week.

The distribution became bimodal: the release sped up the common path and slowed a subset, so the mean improves while the tail grows. Segment by the variable that separates the groups and inspect logs and traces for the slow cohort.
Mean and p95 must move in the same direction, so the divergence means the two panels use different time windows or the percentile query is wrong.
A p95 rise is acceptable while the mean stays under the threshold, because only 5% of requests are above it and the error budget still has room.
mcqs.explanation: A falling mean with a rising p95 is the signature of a skewed or bimodal distribution: a majority got faster while a minority got much slower, and the mean blends both into a single flattering number. The fix is to segment and confirm — device class, route, payment provider, cohort — then open the traces and logs of the slow group, because a percentile describes the distribution, not its cause. The strongest distractor is the outlier story: switching to the median hides the same tail (median is robust precisely because it ignores it), and with a real sample a few extreme requests cannot move p95, so the rise represents a genuine share of users. Expecting mean and p95 to agree assumes a symmetric distribution, and the "only 5%" reading understates the impact — 5% of checkouts is a large number of people, and the comparison belongs against an SLO on a user-facing indicator, not against the mean.

mcqs.question: The team wants error monitoring, tracing and session replay in production. Which plan treats the monitoring SDK as a costed dependency instead of free measurement?
options: Load the full SDK synchronously in `<head>` and sample at 100%, so no error, span or replay is ever missed.
Keep loading the full SDK, but send every event inside `requestIdleCallback`, which moves its cost off the critical path.

Lazy-load an errors-only bundle after the page is interactive, defer tracing and replay until their value justifies the earlier work and sample them, then measure the SDK's resource timing and Core Web Vitals with it enabled and disabled, under size, CPU and event-volume budgets with an owner.
Rely on the vendor's bundle size (for example under 30 kB gzipped), because a script that small cannot affect Core Web Vitals.
mcqs.explanation: The SDK costs more than its download: bytes on the network, parsing and execution on the main thread, memory, outbound telemetry, and the risk of changing the experience it measures. That makes it a budgeted product dependency — so the load is deferred where the debugging need allows (error-only first), heavier signals are sampled, and the cost is verified by comparing vitals and interaction data with the SDK on and off. The strongest distractor is moving sends into `requestIdleCallback`: deferring the transport does not remove the parse, the instrumentation or the serialisation, and it silently drops events when the page is busy or unloaded — the main-thread cost is paid on load, not at send time. A gzipped size proves nothing about main-thread work, and synchronous 100% capture pays all the cost up front on the exact path it is measuring.

scenarios.prompt: During the Friday deploy, ~40 users with an old cart in localStorage hit `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'currency')` inside the cart island's first render. Sentry has exactly one issue for that period: a `ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications` warning, with no `release` and no `environment`. The ticket was closed as 'SDK broken in production'. Review the entry point and the QA note, explain which error paths this code cannot capture, then rewrite the entry point and the verification so a repeat of Friday would be caught.
rubric: Places Friday's failure in the first synchronous render, before the deferred `Sentry.init` ran, so no handler existed yet — and states the boundary precisely instead of 'all early errors'.
Rejects the console throw as verification: it runs in the console's own context and never reaches the SDK's window handlers, so the result proves nothing either way.
Moves init ahead of application code and attaches `environment` and `release` so events can be compared against the previous release.
Verifies from an application code path and checks issue + environment + release + symbolicated frames + breadcrumbs, not merely that an event arrived.
Separates the pipeline check from the ordering check (a forced throw during render in non-production) and keeps cost bounded with errors-first and sampling instead of restoring the deferral.

scenarios.prompt: This is the storefront's entire Core Web Vitals collection. The dashboard reports 'average INP 130 ms — we pass'. Two weeks later, support reports that the product page 'freezes when you tap a size'. Identify what this code reports and why that number cannot answer the question, then rewrite the collection so a p75 per metric is computable.
rubric: Names the mixed-unit average as meaningless: CLS is unitless, LCP and INP are milliseconds on different scales, so no 'average INP' can come out of this array.
States the passing view (p75 per metric against 2.5 s / 200 ms / 0.1) and explains that a mean hides the quarter of sessions with poor interactions.
Reports each metric separately with its identity (name, id, rating) and keeps raw per-visit values, because p75 cannot be recovered from per-pageview means.
Adds segment dimensions (route, device, release) so the slow cohort behind the complaint is findable.
Keeps field collection and `sendBeacon` on `pagehide`, and guards the empty-sample case instead of shipping nulls.

scenarios.prompt: This is the checkout logging running in production. Support can see that orders failed but not which step; a separate ticket flagged that user emails appear in the log export. Refactor the logging so an incident can be answered from the logs — without leaking data, without a transcript, and without losing the failure from error tracking. Keep the function's contract.
rubric: Replaces whole-object dumps with stable named fields (`order_id`, `item_count`, `duration_ms`, `outcome`).
Removes PII (explicit email, full user/cart/order) and places redaction before transport, on the client.
Emits one wide event per operation at the boundary with severity tied to actionability, instead of a start/ok/failed transcript.
Reports the caught error to error tracking while keeping the `Promise<Order>` contract intact.
Adds correlation (trace id plus release) so the log joins its trace, error and replay, and names retention and access as an owner decision outside the client.

scenarios.prompt: This span was added around checkout last sprint. Since then, traces of failed checkouts cannot be found at all, and in traces of successful checkouts the payment request shows up as its own root. Predict what happens on each path, then rewrite the function so the span is correct on every path and the trace keeps the call tree.
rubric: Failure path: `span.end()` is skipped, and an unended span is never exported, so the trace has no `checkout` span and the error is recorded nowhere.
Success path: `startSpan` is not active, so `createOrder`'s request has no parent and becomes its own root trace.
Fix uses `startActiveSpan` and returns its result, preserving the `Promise<Order>` contract.
`finally` ends the span on success, rejection and synchronous throw, with `recordException` plus an error status marking the failure.
Re-throws so callers still see the error, and keeps one stable operation name at the operation boundary instead of a span per function.

scenarios.prompt: Checkout is slower for a subset of users after release `2f1c9ad`: support reports keep arriving, the error rate is flat, and this alert has never fired. Review the detection and the runbook, say what the mean, p75 and p95 would have shown for this window, and rewrite both. Then judge the proposal at the bottom of the ticket.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
The detection is asking a capacity question and calling it an experience question. The mean is 254 ms — (184 × 120 + 16 × 1800) / 200 = 254.4 — comfortably under the 400 ms threshold, so the alert could never fire for this shape of incident: a fast majority subsidises a slow minority inside the same average. The distribution is bimodal. Nearest-rank p75 is 120 ms, while p95 is 1800 ms, because the 190th of 200 sorted values already falls in the slow block: 8% of checkouts wait fifteen times the fast path. The flat error rate is consistent with that — a slow request is not an error, so "no errors" says nothing about latency.

Rewrite the detection around the user condition, not the total. For example: page when p95 exceeds 800 ms for 10 minutes, or when the share of requests above 1 s passes 2%, scoped to route, release and environment so deploy noise does not page. Always attach the window and sample size to the number, keep the mean on a capacity dashboard where it belongs, and keep p75 visible so the majority's experience is still readable next to the tail.

Then give each signal its job. The metric detected and quantified the regression. Traces follow one affected request across boundaries and show which span spent the time — here, the payment provider call — and the parent-child tree is what proves a call is upstream or downstream of the slowdown. Logs explain the discrete event inside that request once it is selected, correlated by trace or request id and carrying stable fields such as `outcome`, `provider`, `duration_ms` and `release`. The current runbook inverts this: grepping `error` and ranking services by matching lines measures how verbose a service is, not how broken it is — a chatty healthy service outranks a quiet failing one, and the slow requests never appear because they produce no error line. Start from the cohort instead: filter requests above 1 s in the window, open their traces, and diff the top span against a fast request from the same release. Check whether payment provider, region, cart shape or account tier separates the two groups, because a percentile is a distribution statement, not a cause, and the segment is the hypothesis to test before shipping a fix.

The proposal is the wrong lesson. Debug logging at the start and end of every function is the highest-cardinality, lowest-signal option: it multiplies volume, buries the one event that matters, multiplies anything sensitive that flows through those objects, and adds main-thread work to the page. Tracing and replay at 100% multiplies bytes, storage, exposure and main-thread execution, and can degrade the INP it is supposed to measure. The bounded version: one wide event per operation at the boundary, traces and replays sampled with an error-biased rate, and a size, CPU and event-volume budget with an owner — plus a decision criterion written before the next deploy, such as "if p95 stays above 800 ms or the slow share above 2% for 10 minutes, revert 2f1c9ad and investigate".
rubric: Computes the numbers instead of gesturing: mean ≈ 254 ms (below the 400 ms threshold, so the alert cannot fire), p95 = 1800 ms against p75 = 120 ms, naming the ~8% slow cohort.
Replaces mean-based paging with a user-facing condition scoped by route, window and release (p95 or share-over-threshold, with a duration), keeping window and sample size attached to the number.
Assigns each signal its job — metric to detect and quantify, correlated logs for the event detail, traces to locate the slow span — and rejects log-volume triage because verbosity is not failure.
Rejects blanket debug logging and 100% tracing/replay on cardinality, cost and measurement grounds, and proposes bounded sampling plus a budget with an owner.
Ends with a confirmation step and a reverting criterion (segment by provider/cohort, compare slow and fast traces, revert if the tail persists) instead of declaring a cause from the percentile.
